WORKERS' RIGHTS IN EMERGENCIES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Inc.

ABOUT THIS WORKERS' RIGHTS IN EMERGENCIES INFORMATION SHEET
This Workers' Rights in Emergencies — Information Sheet describes California Labor Code section 1139, a statute added by SB 1044 (Stats. 2022, ch. 829) that took effect January 1, 2023, as that statute relates to the working relationship between Jane Doe and Acme Inc.

Section 1139 does two specific things: first, it bars an employer from taking or threatening adverse action against an employee for refusing to report to, or leaving, a workplace or worksite within an area affected by an "emergency condition" (a defined term covering natural-disaster or criminal-act peril, or an evacuation order) where the employee has a reasonable belief the workplace or worksite is unsafe; second, it bars an employer from preventing an employee from accessing a mobile device or other communications device during an emergency condition to seek help, assess safety, or check on someone's safety. The statute lists thirteen categories of employees to whom the first protection does not apply, ties the employee's notice duty to whether advance notice is feasible, and states that it is not intended to apply once an emergency condition's imminent and ongoing risk has ceased.

This is narrower than it may sound. Section 1139's own text does not create a paid-leave entitlement, an accrual bank, a certification or medical-documentation process, a minimum-service or employer-size eligibility threshold, or a job-guarantee/reinstatement right of the kind found in leave statutes such as the California Family Rights Act or the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act paid sick leave law — both covered by this corpus's own separate information sheets. It is, on its own text, an anti-retaliation and device-access statute keyed to a specific factual trigger (an emergency condition), not a scheduled or approved absence benefit. It is also distinct from this corpus's Right to Refuse Hazardous Work information sheet, which describes a different, older statute (Labor Code §§ 6310-6312) tied to a safety-standard violation rather than to a natural-disaster, criminal-act, or evacuation-order emergency condition, and from this corpus's Workplace Violence Prevention Plan information sheet, which describes an employer's affirmative planning duty rather than an individual employee's right to leave or refuse to report.

This information sheet states facts about what section 1139's own text says. It is not legal advice, does not determine that any "emergency condition" exists or existed at any particular time or place, does not determine that any employee's belief that a workplace or worksite was unsafe was or was not reasonable, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney or the California Labor Commissioner's Office about a specific situation.

THE DEFINED TERM "EMERGENCY CONDITION"
Labor Code section 1139 applies only when an "emergency condition" exists, and the statute defines that term specifically rather than leaving it to general usage. The statute's own text defines it as either of two things: conditions of disaster or extreme peril to the safety of persons or property at the workplace or worksite caused by natural forces or a criminal act, or an order to evacuate a workplace, a worksite, a worker's home, or the school of a worker's child due to natural disaster or a criminal act. The statute's own text then expressly carves out one thing the term does not include: a health pandemic. This chapter's protections accordingly do not extend, by the statute's own terms, to a pandemic-driven workplace-safety dispute, however serious.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Emergency condition” means the existence of either of the following: (i) Conditions of disaster or extreme peril to the safety of persons or property at the workplace or worksite caused by natural forces or a criminal act. (ii) An order to evacuate a workplace, a worksite, a worker’s home, or the school of a worker’s child due to natural disaster or a criminal act."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  "“Emergency condition” does not include a health pandemic."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(a)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text does not further define "extreme peril," "disaster," or how localized or widespread a natural-forces or criminal-act condition must be to qualify, and this research session did not independently verify any published California appellate decision construing those terms because a CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) rather than results, so this clause states only what the statute's own text says. This document does not determine that any particular event was or was not an "emergency condition" within the statute's definition.

THE "REASONABLE BELIEF THE WORKPLACE IS UNSAFE" STANDARD
Beyond an emergency condition existing at all, section 1139's core protection also depends on whether the employee had "a reasonable belief that the workplace or worksite is unsafe." The statute's own text defines this as an objective standard measured from the vantage point of a reasonable person under the circumstances known to the employee at the time, concluding there is a real danger of death or serious injury from entering or remaining on the premises — not simply a subjective fear, and not simply any risk. The statute's own text also identifies one specific factor relevant to that objective inquiry: whether health and safety regulations specific to the emergency condition exist, whether the employer complied or failed to comply with them, and whether that information was known to the employee or the employee received legally mandated training on those regulations at the relevant time.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“A reasonable belief that the workplace or worksite is unsafe” means that a reasonable person, under the circumstances known to the employee at the time, would conclude there is a real danger of death or serious injury if that person enters or remains on the premises."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  "The existence of any health and safety regulations specific to the emergency condition and an employer’s compliance or noncompliance with those regulations shall be a relevant factor if this information is known to the employee at the time of the emergency condition or the employee received training on the health and safety regulations mandated by law specific to the emergency condition."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text describes this specific-regulation-compliance fact as "a relevant factor," not as the exclusive or a dispositive one, and does not otherwise enumerate what other facts bear on "reasonable belief" or on "real danger of death or serious injury." This research session did not independently verify any published California appellate decision applying this standard, for the reason disclosed in the companion definitions clause (a CourtListener rate-limit error). This document does not determine that any specific employee's belief was or was not reasonable in any specific circumstance.

THE CORE RIGHT — NO ADVERSE ACTION FOR REFUSING TO REPORT OR LEAVING DURING AN EMERGENCY CONDITION
The statute's own text states the core prohibition as follows: in the event of an emergency condition, an employer may not take or threaten adverse action against an employee for refusing to report to, or leaving, a workplace or worksite within the affected area because the employee has a reasonable belief the workplace or worksite is unsafe. Read on its own terms, this is an anti-retaliation rule tied to a specific act (refusing to report, or leaving) and a specific belief (reasonable belief of unsafety during an emergency condition) — it does not, by its own text, obligate an employer to pay the employee for time not worked as a result, and it does not itself require the employer to excuse the absence as a category of paid or unpaid leave with its own accrual or scheduling mechanics.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In the event of an emergency condition, an employer shall not do either of the following: (1) Take or threaten adverse action against any employee for refusing to report to, or leaving, a workplace or worksite within the affected area because the employee has a reasonable belief that the workplace or worksite is unsafe."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text does not define "the affected area," "adverse action," or "threaten," leaving the geographic and conduct scope of the protection to be worked out case by case; this research session did not independently verify any published California appellate decision construing those terms, for the reason disclosed in the companion definitions clause (a CourtListener rate-limit error). This protection is also subject to the thirteen categorical exemptions described in a companion clause, which this clause does not restate. This document does not determine that any specific refusal or departure was or was not protected in any specific case.

THIRTEEN CATEGORIES OF EMPLOYEES TO WHOM THE CORE RIGHT DOES NOT APPLY
The statute's own text states that the refuse-to-report/leave protection above does not apply to thirteen listed categories of employees, introduced by the phrase "This paragraph does not apply to the following," followed by items (A) through (M). Those items are, by the statute's own description: first responders as defined by Government Code section 8562; disaster service workers as defined by Government Code section 3101; employees required by law to render aid or remain on the premises during an emergency; employees or contractors of a health care facility who provide direct patient care, support patient care operations during an emergency, or are required by law or policy to participate in emergency response or evacuation; employees of a private entity contracting with government to provide or aid emergency services; employees working on a military base or in the defense industrial base sector; employees performing essential work on nuclear reactors or nuclear materials or waste; employees of a utility, communications, energy, or roadside-assistance company while actively engaged in or called upon to aid emergency response, including maintaining public access to services such as energy and water; employees of a licensed residential care facility; employees of a depository institution as defined by Financial Code section 1420; transportation employees participating directly in emergency evacuations during an active evacuation; employees of a privately contracted private fire prevention resource operating as a "qualified insurance resource" under specified Health and Safety Code provisions; and employees whose primary duties include assisting members of the public to evacuate during an emergency.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This paragraph does not apply to the following: (A) A first responder, as defined in Section 8562 of the Government Code. (B) A disaster service worker, as defined in Section 3101 of the Government Code."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(b)(1)(A)-(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  "(M) An employee whose primary duties include assisting members of the public to evacuate in case of an emergency."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(b)(1)(M) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  Known gap: This research session fetched and verified Labor Code section 1139's own text describing these thirteen categories, but did not independently fetch or verify the cross-referenced definitions in Government Code sections 8562 and 3101, Financial Code section 1420, or the Health and Safety Code provisions on qualified insurance resources; whether a specific employee falls within one of these categories can turn on those other statutes' own definitions, which this document does not independently confirm. This document does not determine that any specific employee is or is not within an exempt category.

A SEPARATE RIGHT — ACCESS TO A COMMUNICATIONS DEVICE DURING AN EMERGENCY CONDITION
Section 1139 states a second, textually separate prohibition from the refuse-to-report/leave right above: during an emergency condition, an employer may not prevent an employee from accessing the employee's mobile device or other communications device for seeking emergency assistance, assessing the safety of the situation, or communicating with a person to verify their safety. The statute's own text extends this device-access protection to public-sector employees as well as employees of private entities — specifically, to any employee of the state or of a city, county, or political subdivision, including a special district. The statute's own text then exempts three narrower categories from the device-access right: employees of a depository institution as defined by Financial Code section 1420, employees of any correctional facility, and employees actively operating equipment permitted under specified provisions of the Business and Professions Code (governing private investigators, private security services, and related licensed activities).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Prevent any employee from accessing the employee’s mobile device or other communications device for seeking emergency assistance, assessing the safety of the situation, or communicating with a person to verify their safety."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(b)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  "In addition to employees of private entities, this paragraph applies to any employee of the state or any city, county, or political subdivision of the state, including a special district."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(b)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text does not define "prevent," and does not specify whether a generally applicable device-use or device-storage policy that is not aimed at emergencies would itself "prevent" access within the meaning of this provision. This research session did not independently fetch or verify the cross-referenced Business and Professions Code provisions defining the equipment-operation exemption. This document does not determine that any specific employer practice does or does not violate this provision.

THE EMPLOYEE'S NOTICE DUTY
Section 1139 conditions the refuse-to-report/leave protection on a notice duty, but structures that duty around feasibility rather than requiring notice in every case. The statute's own text states that when feasible, an employee shall notify the employer of the emergency condition requiring the employee to leave or refuse to report to the workplace or worksite prior to leaving or refusing to report; and that when prior notice is not feasible, the employee shall instead notify the employer of the emergency condition after leaving or refusing to report, as soon as possible.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(1) When feasible, an employee shall notify the employer of the emergency condition requiring the employee to leave or refuse to report to the workplace or worksite prior to leaving or refusing to report. (2) When prior notice described by paragraph (1) is not feasible, the employee shall notify the employer of the emergency condition that required the employee to leave or refuse to report to the workplace or worksite after leaving or refusing to report as soon as possible."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text does not specify the form the notice must take (written, verbal, or otherwise), to whom at the employer it must be directed, or what consequence follows if an employee's notice is late, incomplete, or omitted where notice was in fact feasible. This document does not determine whether any specific employee's notice, or lack of notice, satisfied this duty in any specific case.

WHEN THE PROTECTION STOPS APPLYING
The statute's own text places a temporal limit on itself: section 1139 is not intended to apply once emergency conditions that pose an imminent and ongoing risk of harm to the workplace, the worksite, the worker, or the worker's home have ceased. Read together with the notice-duty clause above, the protection is tied to the period during which the imminent and ongoing risk exists, not to a fixed number of days or to the underlying disaster event's total duration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This section is not intended to apply when emergency conditions that pose an imminent and ongoing risk of harm to the workplace, the worksite, the worker, or the worker’s home have ceased."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text does not define when an emergency condition's "imminent and ongoing risk of harm" has "ceased," including in a case where an underlying disaster (for example, a wildfire or flood) continues in the broader area but no longer poses an imminent, ongoing risk to a specific workplace or worksite. This document does not determine that any specific emergency condition had or had not ceased at any particular time.

ENFORCEMENT — PAGA AND THE EMPLOYER'S RIGHT TO CURE
Section 1139's own text does not create its own standalone civil-penalty or complaint procedure; the only enforcement mechanism its text specifically addresses is a Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA) civil action. The statute's own text states that in any PAGA action a current or former employee could bring for a violation of this chapter, the employer has the right to cure the alleged violation as set forth in a separate statute, Labor Code section 2699.3. Section 2699.3's own text, independently fetched for this document, in turn sets out more than one differently structured pre-suit notice and cure procedure depending on which Labor Code provision is at issue and, for one of those procedures, the employer's number of employees; the version of that procedure applicable to a violation of a provision (such as section 1139) that is not listed in Labor Code section 2699.5 and is not part of Division 5 (the occupational safety and health division) lets an employer that employed fewer than 100 employees during the notice period submit a confidential cure proposal to the Labor and Workforce Development Agency within 33 days of the employee's notice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In any action by a current or former employee that could be brought pursuant to the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act of 2004 (Part 13 (commencing with Section 2698)) for violations of this chapter, the employer shall have the right to cure alleged violations as set forth in Section 2699.3."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1139(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1139.)
  "an employer that employed fewer than 100 employees in total during the period covered by the notice may submit to the agency a confidential proposal to cure one or more of the alleged violations"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2699.3(c)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2699.3.)
  Known gap: This research session did not independently fetch or verify Labor Code section 2699.5's own list of provisions to confirm that section 1139 is (or is not) omitted from that list, which is what determines whether the fewer-than-100-employees cure procedure quoted here, rather than a different procedure elsewhere in section 2699.3, actually governs a given chapter 11 PAGA claim; that determination is left undone here rather than assumed. This research session also did not independently verify any published court decision applying section 2699.3's cure procedure to a section 1139 claim specifically, because a CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) during this session. This document does not determine that any specific employer's cure attempt was or was not sufficient, and does not describe any non-PAGA remedy (such as a Labor Commissioner retaliation complaint) that may or may not separately be available for a section 1139 violation.

expectedJSON.body: The statute's own text places a temporal limit on itself: section 1139 is not intended to apply once emergency conditions that pose an imminent and ongoing risk of harm to the workplace, the worksite, the worker, or the worker's home have ceased. Read together with the notice-duty clause above, the protection is tied to the period during which the imminent and ongoing risk exists, not to a fixed number of days or to the underlying disaster event's total duration.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: This section is not intended to apply when emergency conditions that pose an imminent and ongoing risk of harm to the workplace, the worksite, the worker, or the worker’s home have ceased.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute's own text does not define when an emergency condition's "imminent and ongoing risk of harm" has "ceased," including in a case where an underlying disaster (for example, a wildfire or flood) continues in the broader area but no longer poses an imminent, ongoing risk to a specific workplace or worksite. This document does not determine that any specific emergency condition had or had not ceased at any particular time.

expectedJSON.body: Section 1139's own text does not create its own standalone civil-penalty or complaint procedure; the only enforcement mechanism its text specifically addresses is a Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA) civil action. The statute's own text states that in any PAGA action a current or former employee could bring for a violation of this chapter, the employer has the right to cure the alleged violation as set forth in a separate statute, Labor Code section 2699.3. Section 2699.3's own text, independently fetched for this document, in turn sets out more than one differently structured pre-suit notice and cure procedure depending on which Labor Code provision is at issue and, for one of those procedures, the employer's number of employees; the version of that procedure applicable to a violation of a provision (such as section 1139) that is not listed in Labor Code section 2699.5 and is not part of Division 5 (the occupational safety and health division) lets an employer that employed fewer than 100 employees during the notice period submit a confidential cure proposal to the Labor and Workforce Development Agency within 33 days of the employee's notice.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: In any action by a current or former employee that could be brought pursuant to the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act of 2004 (Part 13 (commencing with Section 2698)) for violations of this chapter, the employer shall have the right to cure alleged violations as set forth in Section 2699.3.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2699.3(c)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: an employer that employed fewer than 100 employees in total during the period covered by the notice may submit to the agency a confidential proposal to cure one or more of the alleged violations

expectedJSON.gap: This research session did not independently fetch or verify Labor Code section 2699.5's own list of provisions to confirm that section 1139 is (or is not) omitted from that list, which is what determines whether the fewer-than-100-employees cure procedure quoted here, rather than a different procedure elsewhere in section 2699.3, actually governs a given chapter 11 PAGA claim; that determination is left undone here rather than assumed. This research session also did not independently verify any published court decision applying section 2699.3's cure procedure to a section 1139 claim specifically, because a CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) during this session. This document does not determine that any specific employer's cure attempt was or was not sufficient, and does not describe any non-PAGA remedy (such as a Labor Commissioner retaliation complaint) that may or may not separately be available for a section 1139 violation.
